citations.title: Python Exercise Guide
citations.text:
Exercise Set B: Functions and Collections
Exercise B1. Write a function average(numbers) that returns the arithmetic mean of a list. Handle an empty list by returning None instead of dividing by zero.
Exercise B2. Count word frequency. Given a sentence, build a dictionary mapping each lowercase word to its count. Use counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1. Alternative: collections.Counter.
Exercise B3. Remove duplicates from a list while preserving order. Converting to a set removes duplicates but loses ordering; use a seen set and an output list, or dict.fromkeys(items).
Exercise B4. Explain why the following function is buggy: def add_item(item, items=[]): items.append(item); return items. Answer: the default list is created once and shared between calls, so items accumulate across calls. The fix is to use None as the default.

S3.title: Python Lecture Notes
S3.text: count from the end, so "python"[-1] is "n". Slicing "python"[1:4] returns "yth" (start included, stop excluded).  F-strings embed expressions inside text: f"Total: {price * 2:.2f}" formats a number with two decimals. Integer division // discards the fractional part (7 // 2 is 3), the modulo operator % returns the remainder (7 % 2 is 1), and ** is exponentiation (2 ** 10 is 1024). Dividing with / always returns a float, so 6 / 3 is 2.0.

S4.title: Python Glossary Overloaded Terms
S4.text: program prints the same random numbers on every run. iterable: an object you can loop over, such as a list or string.  An iterator is the object that produces the values one at a time and is returned by iter(iterable). generator: a function that uses yield to produce values lazily, one at a time, instead of building a whole list in memory. decorator: a function that wraps another function; written with the @ syntax above a def line. mean: Python has no built-in mean. Use statistics.mean(data), or statistics.fmean(data) for a faster floating-point mean.

S5.title: Statistics Robust Summaries
S5.text:
The mean is the sum of the values divided by their count, so every value, including extreme ones,
pulls it. The median is the middle value of the sorted data and ignores how far the extremes lie.
When a distribution is right-skewed (a long tail of a few very large values, as with prices or
incomes) a few large values drag the mean upward while the median stays near the typical value, so
the mean exceeds the median. When the data are symmetric the two are close. A large gap between the
mean and the median is therefore a quick diagnostic for skew or outliers. For skewed data, report
the median (or both) because it better describes a typical observation.
S5.location: ROBUST SUMMARIES: WHY THE MEAN AND THE MEDIAN DIFFER
